You revise one blog article for an online shop. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, the current draft, and the problems found in it. Return the whole article again with every problem fixed. Where a sentence cannot be backed by a fact, remove it or say less; never add a citation the fact does not support. Keep what was good.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Beans, Grind, Ratio and Steep Time
Meta description: Learn how to make cold brew coffee at home: choosing beans, grinding coarse, getting the ratio and steep time right, then filtering, diluting and storing.
Slug: how-to-make-cold-brew-coffee-at-home

To make cold brew coffee, steep coarsely ground coffee in cold water for many hours, then remove the grounds and dilute the concentrate to taste. Most home recipes call for a steep of roughly 12 to 24 hours in the fridge or at room temperature [G]. Four variables decide the result: the beans, the grind size, the ratio of coffee to water and the steep time. Get those right and the rest is simply patience.

## What cold brew is and why it tastes different

Cold brew is an immersion method. Instead of water passing through a bed of coffee, as in pour-over, the grounds sit fully submerged in the water for the whole brew. The difference from a hot immersion brew such as a French press is temperature: cold water extracts far more slowly, so a brew that takes minutes when hot takes hours when cold.

That slow, cool extraction changes the flavour. Hot water pulls out acids and volatile aromatics quickly, along with some of the harsher compounds that read as bitterness. Cold water extracts more selectively, so cold brew usually tastes rounder, sweeter and lower in perceived acidity, with a heavier, almost syrupy body.

It is worth separating cold brew from iced coffee. Iced coffee is coffee brewed hot and then chilled or poured over ice, which keeps the brightness and aromatics of a hot brew but can taste thin or sharp once diluted. Cold brew never meets hot water at all, which is why the two drinks taste so different even when both are served over ice.

You can make cold brew in almost any vessel, but a dedicated brewer makes the process cleaner. Our [Cold Brew Jar](P1) is an immersion brewer made by Fernhill for exactly this job [F2, F3].

{{P1}}

## Choosing beans for cold brew

Because cold extraction mutes acidity and emphasises body and sweetness, the classic choice is a medium roast with chocolate, caramel and nut character. These coffees are forgiving: even if your ratio or steep time is a little off, the cup stays smooth and sweet. Lighter, fruit-forward roasts work too, but they give a brighter, more unusual cold brew, which some people love and others find surprising.

In our range, the dependable pick is [Colombia Huila, washed](P2), a washed-process, medium-roast single origin [F11, F20, F15]. Its tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate suit the rounded, sweet profile that cold brew brings out [F22]. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg bags, and the larger size makes sense if cold brew becomes a regular habit [F14].

{{P2}}

For something more adventurous, [Ethiopia Guji, natural process](P4) is a light roast with notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F41, F42]. As cold brew it tends towards a fruity, almost wine-like concentrate rather than a classic chocolatey one.

Whichever coffee you choose, buy it whole bean and grind it yourself. Ethiopia Guji is sold as whole bean, filter grind or espresso grind, and for cold brew the whole bean option is the one to choose [F35]. A pre-ground filter grind is too fine for a steep that lasts many hours, and it will push your concentrate towards bitterness. You can browse all of our single origins in the [coffee beans collection](L3).

## Grind coarse, like for French press

Grind size matters more in cold brew than in almost any other method, simply because the coffee sits in water for so long. Small differences in particle size are magnified over a long steep.

- **Too fine:** the coffee over-extracts, tasting bitter, woody or harsh, and fine particles cloud the concentrate and clog the filter, giving a muddy result.
- **Too coarse:** the water cannot extract enough from each particle, and the concentrate tastes weak, sour or hollow even after a long steep.
- **Just right:** a coarse, even grind similar to what you would use for a French press, with particles roughly the size of coarse sea salt.

A burr grinder gives the most even particle size, which is what keeps cold brew clean. Our [Hand Grinder](P3) uses conical steel burrs and has external click adjustment with 30 settings [F23, F26]. Its settings run from espresso to French press, so the coarse end of the dial covers cold brew [F27].

Be aware of one practical point. The Hand Grinder holds 25 g of beans at a time, so a full basket of up to 150 g for the Cold Brew Jar takes several rounds of grinding [F28, F6]. Set your coarse setting once, then grind in batches into the same container so every load matches. More grinders, including electric models, are in our [grinders collection](L2).

{{P3}}

## How much coffee and how long to steep

Cold brew is usually made as a concentrate, then diluted before drinking, though you can also brew it ready to drink. As a general guide, measured by weight:

- **Concentrate:** roughly 1:5 to 1:8 coffee to water [G].
- **Ready to drink:** around 1:12 to 1:15 coffee to water [G].

Weighing both the coffee and the water with a scale, rather than using scoops and jug markings, is what lets you repeat a good batch and adjust a disappointing one with precision. Change one variable at a time, either the dose or the steep time, so you know which change made the difference.

The Cold Brew Jar is built around a concentrate batch. Its filter basket holds up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee, and the jar makes 1.5 litres of concentrate [F6, F7]. The recommended steep time is 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F10]. Begin in the middle of that window, taste, and adjust on the next batch: steep longer if the concentrate tastes thin or sour, and shorter if it tastes bitter or flat. A fuller basket gives a stronger concentrate, while a lighter dose gives a softer one you can dilute less.

## Step by step with the Cold Brew Jar

1. **Weigh and grind.** Weigh your beans, up to the basket's limit of 150 g, and grind them coarse [F6].
2. **Fill the basket.** Tip the grounds into the fine stainless steel filter basket and level them gently [F5].
3. **Add water slowly.** Pour cold, filtered water slowly over the grounds so every particle is wetted; dry pockets extract unevenly. Give the grounds a gentle stir if any stay dry on top.
4. **Seal it.** Close the airtight lid to keep fridge odours out and the brew fresh [F8].
5. **Refrigerate.** The jar fits in a fridge door, so it does not take over a shelf while it steeps [F9].
6. **Steep.** Leave it for 12 to 18 hours in the fridge, as recommended [F10]. Because the jar is glass, you can check the colour of the brew at a glance [F4].
7. **Lift out the basket.** When the time is up, remove the filter basket and let it drain. Taking the grounds out of the water is what stops extraction, so do not leave the basket in once the steep is done.

What is left in the jar is your concentrate, ready to dilute and serve.

## Diluting, serving and storing your concentrate

A good starting point is to dilute concentrate about 1:1 with cold water or milk, poured over ice [G]. From there, adjust to taste: add more water for a lighter, more refreshing glass, or less for something closer to an iced espresso drink. Milk and oat milk both pair well with the chocolatey sweetness of a medium-roast cold brew.

A few ideas once you have the basics:

- **Cold brew tonic:** pour concentrate over tonic water and ice for a bitter-sweet, sparkling drink that suits fruity, light-roast coffees especially well.
- **Hot cold brew:** dilute the concentrate with just-boiled water for a smooth, low-acidity hot cup.
- **Sweetened:** stir in simple syrup rather than granulated sugar, which dissolves poorly in cold liquid.

For storage, keep the concentrate sealed and cold. The Cold Brew Jar's airtight lid means the concentrate can stay in the same jar it brewed in [F8]. Undiluted concentrate is generally best drunk within about a week to ten days, after which the flavour starts to fade and turn stale [G]. Dilute only what you are about to drink, as diluted cold brew loses its character faster.

## No dedicated jar? Use a French press

If you already own a French press, or want one brewer that handles both hot and cold coffee, you can make cold brew in it. Our [French Press](P6) is an immersion brewer with a capacity of 1 litre, which makes it suited to a smaller batch than a dedicated cold brew jar [F53, F52].

1. Add coarse grounds to the beaker and pour in cold, filtered water, stirring gently so everything is wet.
2. Rest the lid on top without pressing, cover the spout, and steep it in the fridge.
3. When the steep is done, press the plunger down slowly.
4. Decant the coffee into a separate sealed bottle straight away, because coffee left sitting on the grounds keeps extracting and turns bitter.

The French Press has a four-layer mesh filter, which holds back the coarse grounds when you press [F58]. Expect a little more fine sediment than from a dedicated filter basket, so pour gently and leave the last of the liquid behind. Afterwards, all parts come apart for cleaning, which helps after a long steep [F59]. You can compare it with the Cold Brew Jar in our [immersion brewers collection](L4).

{{P6}}

Whichever brewer you use, the method is the same: good beans, an even coarse grind, a weighed ratio and a patient steep. Nail those four, and a fridge full of smooth homemade cold brew is only ever one evening's prep away.
</draft>

<problems>
1. review, grounding 3/5: Most product sentences match their cited facts. One uncited, unsupported claim about how the Ethiopia Guji behaves as cold brew, and a few benefits stretched beyond the facts.
2. "As cold brew it tends towards a fruity, almost wine-like concentrate rather than a classic chocolatey one." — Product claim about the Ethiopia Guji's cold brew character has no supporting fact and no citation. The facts list only roast level and tasting notes.
3. "The Cold Brew Jar is built around a concentrate batch. Its filter basket holds up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee, and the jar makes 1.5 litres of concentrate [F6, F7]." — 150 g to 1.5 litres is about 1:10, outside the 1:5 to 1:8 concentrate range the article just gave. This is an internal inconsistency the reader is left to resolve.
4. "Close the airtight lid to keep fridge odours out and the brew fresh [F8]." — F8 says only that the lid is airtight. Keeping odours out and the brew fresh is an implied benefit that goes beyond the fact.
5. "Expect a little more fine sediment than from a dedicated filter basket, so pour gently and leave the last of the liquid behind." — Comparative performance claim between the French Press and the Cold Brew Jar is not supported by any fact.
6. "Undiluted concentrate is generally best drunk within about a week to ten days, after which the flavour starts to fade and turn stale [G]." — Marked as general knowledge, but shelf-life guidance varies by source (often under two weeks, sometimes shorter). The figure is soft.
</problems>
